title: Recursion
misconceptions: A recursive function runs faster and uses less memory than an equivalent iterative loop.
When a recursive function calls itself, it reuses and overwrites the exact same local variables in memory.
The return value from the base case automatically jumps back to the original outer caller without unwinding through intermediate function calls.
Infinite recursion will run forever in a loop without causing a program crash.
A base case is optional if the function uses a conditional loop to stop executing.

rubric.text: Defines recursion as a method where a function calls itself directly or indirectly to solve a larger problem by breaking it into smaller instances.
Explains that every valid recursive function requires at least one base case that produces a result without making further recursive calls.
Explains that the recursive step must modify input arguments to bring subsequent subproblems strictly closer to a base case.
Describes how each recursive call pushes a new stack frame onto the execution call stack to maintain distinct local variables and execution state.
Explains the unwinding phase, where control and return values flow backward through the stack frame instances after hitting a base case.
Identifies stack overflow as a runtime error caused by exceeding memory limits when recursive calls continue infinitely or too deeply.
Compares time and space complexity of recursive solutions against iterative alternatives, noting memory overhead from stack frames.
Explains tail recursion as a special form where the recursive call is the final operation, enabling tail-call optimization by reusing stack frames.
